links.note: 201 says those practised in evil do not fear 'தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு' while the excellent (விழுமியார்) do. 428 gives the general rule in the chapter on understanding: not fearing what is to be feared (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை) is folly, and fearing it is 'அறிவார் தொழில்'. Read together, the fear in 201 is a working of knowledge and not timidity; Parimelazhagar on 428 lists sin, blame and ruin among the things to be feared.

Both end on the phrase 'என்னும் செருக்கு'. In 201 it is 'தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு', which Parimelazhagar glosses as a delusion (மயக்கம்) and Manakkudavar as an exhilaration (களிப்பு) that the good fear; in 180 it is 'வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு', the pride of not wanting, which yields victory (விறல்). The same word names a heady state to be dreaded in one verse and a state worth having in the other, depending on what it rests on.

201 makes fear of evil deeds the mark of the excellent. 244 says that for one who sustains living beings and practises அருள் there are no deeds his own life need fear ('தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை இல்'). The fear 201 commends is aimed at one's own possible deeds, and 244 names the condition under which nothing of that kind remains to be feared.

202 says evil deeds are to be feared more than fire ('தீயினும் அஞ்சப்படும்') because they yield evil. 129 sets fire against the tongue: a wound burned by fire heals, the scar burned by the tongue does not ('ஆறாதே நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு'). In both, fire is the harm that ends, used to measure a harm that lasts; Parimelazhagar on 202 makes this explicit, saying fire cannot follow one into another time, place or body.

202 ranks evil deeds above fire as a thing to fear. 896, in the Book of Wealth, says one burned by fire may still survive ('எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம்') but those who keep wronging the great will not. The same comparison, fire as the survivable danger, is applied once to one's own deeds and once to the anger of the powerful.

203 calls it the chief of all understanding to refrain from doing evil even to those who hate one ('செறுவார்க்கும் செய்யா விடல்'). 312 says that not hurting in return even one who has hurt you out of hatred ('கறுத்து இன்னா செய்த அக்கண்ணும்') is the settled stand of the stainless. The same rule is called knowledge (அறிவு) in the householder's chapter and purity (மாசற்றார் கோள்) in the ascetic's.

203 puts non-retaliation at the head of understanding ('அறிவினுள் எல்லாம் தலை'). 315 asks what understanding achieves at all ('அறிவினான் ஆகுவது உண்டோ') if one does not guard another's pain as one's own. 315 supplies a reason 203 leaves unstated: understanding is measured by how one treats others' pain, so harming even an enemy shows a failure of it.

203 asks only for restraint: do no evil even to enemies. 987 asks what worth (சால்பு) is good for if it does not do pleasant things even to those who did one harm ('இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்'). The Book of Wealth's ideal of the சான்றோர் goes one step beyond the householder's rule, from not returning harm to returning good.

In 204 அறம் is an agent that plots the ruin of anyone who plots another's ('அறம் சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு'). In 130 அறம் is again an agent, this time watching for the right moment to come to the man who has guarded against anger and learned restraint ('செவ்வி அறம் பார்க்கும்'). Parimelazhagar reads both as அறக்கடவுள்; the pair shows the same personified virtue seeking out a person for ruin in one case and for favour in the other.

204 forbids even contemplating another's ruin, even by a lapse ('மறந்தும் பிறன்கேடு சூழற்க'). 282 says that even to think in the heart of stealing another's goods is wrong ('உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும் தீதே'). Both place the fault at the thought, before any act, one for harm and one for theft.

204 says that if one plots another's ruin, virtue plots one's own. 319 states the return in terms of time: harm done to others in the forenoon brings harm to oneself in the afternoon, of itself ('பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்'). 319's 'தாமே' leaves the return impersonal where 204 gives it an agent, and Parimelazhagar on 204 adds the same point about speed: virtue begins plotting at the very moment the plotter does.

205 forbids doing evil on the plea 'I have nothing' ('இலன் என்று'), since it only makes one poor again. 174 says those of faultless sight who have mastered the senses will not covet on the thought 'we have nothing' ('இலமென்று'). The same excuse is refused in both; 205 answers it with the consequence, 174 with the kind of person who never offers it.

205 rules out poverty as a ground for evil deeds. 656 takes the hardest case: even if one must see the mother who bore one go hungry ('ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்'), one should not do what the worthy condemn. Parimelazhagar notes that 656 sets aside a general rule of the dharma texts allowing wrong to feed one's dependants, which shows how far 205's principle is taken.

205 quotes the plea 'இலன் என்று' as an excuse for wrongdoing. 1040 quotes the same plea, 'இலமென்று', as an excuse for sitting idle, and says the good woman called Land laughs at those who make it. The book hears 'I have nothing' twice as a pretext, once for evil and once for sloth, and rejects it both times.

206: one who does not want afflicting things to overpower him ('நோய்ப்பால தன்னை அடல் வேண்டாதான்') should not do evil to others. 320: all pains rest on those who caused pain, so those who want freedom from pain cause none ('நோய் செய்யார் நோயின்மை வேண்டுபவர்'). The claim and its form (நோய், வேண்டு-) are nearly the same, stated once for the householder in the chapter on fearing evil deeds and once among the ascetic virtues.

206 gives a self-regarding reason for not harming others: the harm comes back on oneself. 316 gives a different ground: what one has oneself perceived as painful ('இன்னா எனத் தான் உணர்ந்தவை') one must not do to another. 206 alone could read as prudence; 316 shows the book also rests the same rule on knowing the other's pain from one's own.

207: whatever enmity people incur they survive ('உய்வர்'), but the enmity of deeds does not leave and follows to kill. 110: those who destroy any other good have an escape ('உய்வுண்டாம்'), but there is none ('உய்வில்லை') for one who destroys a kindness done to him. Both use the same figure, everything else can be escaped except this, to single out one thing: evil deeds in general in 207, ingratitude in 110.

207 treats one's evil deeds as an enemy ('வினைப்பகை') worse than any outward one. 434, advising the king, says fault itself is the enemy that brings ruin ('குற்றமே அற்றம் தரூஉம் பகை') and so guarding against fault should be one's aim. The two verses, one in the Book of Virtue and one in the Book of Wealth, both move the real enemy from outside to one's own conduct.

207 says the enmity of deeds does not leave and follows behind to kill ('வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்'). 208 gives the image for it: the ruin of evildoers is like a person's shadow that does not leave and stays at the foot ('வீயாது அடி உறைந்தற்று'). The repeated 'வீயாது' ties them, and both Manakkudavar and Parimelazhagar say 208 illustrates what 207 asserted.

208: the ruin of those who did evil is like a shadow that never leaves a person. 36: virtue done now is, at the time one perishes, a companion that does not perish ('பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை'). Both say a person's deeds stay with him; the good deed stays as a companion and the evil deed's ruin as a shadow at his heel.

208 uses a simile of something that cannot fail to happen: ruin stays with the evildoer as his shadow stays at his foot. 307 does the same for anger: the ruin of one who treats anger as a thing of worth is like the hand of one who strikes the ground, which cannot miss ('கை பிழையாதற்று'). Both verses take 'கேடு' as their subject and end on a simile of certainty, one for evil deeds and one for anger.

209: if a person loves himself ('தன்னைத்தான் காதலன் ஆயின்'), let him not go near evil deeds, however small. 305: if you would guard yourself ('தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின்'), guard against anger, or anger will kill you yourself. Both open with the same conditional about one's own self and argue from self-interest, one against evil deeds and one against anger.

209 assumes that doing evil is acting against oneself: one who loves himself stays away from it. 843 says the suffering that those without understanding inflict on themselves is hard even for their enemies ('செறுவார்க்கும்') to inflict. 843 describes the person who fails 209's test, and Parimelazhagar's comment there names poverty, blame and sin as what such people bring on themselves.

210 says that one who does not stray aside and do evil is 'அருங்கேடன்', a person for whom ruin is rare or, in Parimelazhagar's gloss, absent. 169 admits that the upright man's ruin ('செவ்வியான் கேடும்') and the crooked-hearted man's prosperity occur and must be thought about ('நினைக்கப்படும்'). They conflict if 210 is read, with Parimelazhagar and Kalaignar, as promising no ruin at all in this life; Parimelazhagar resolves 169 by referring such cases to deeds of earlier births.

210 promises that the one who does no evil will not come to ruin. 117 says the world will not count as ruin ('கெடுவாக வையாது') the low state (தாழ்வு) of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. 117 allows that the upright may be brought low and changes what counts as 'கேடு', which limits how literally 210's promise can be taken.

210: know ('அறிக') that one who does not turn aside to do evil has no ruin. 116: if one's heart leaves what is fair and does wrong, let one know ('அறிக') 'I shall perish' ('கெடுவல் யான்'). They state the same law from its two sides with the same imperative, 210 for the one who keeps straight and 116 for the one who leaves the middle.

211 says obligation (கடப்பாடு) wants no return, and asks what the world does for the rain in exchange ('என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ'). 101, on gratitude, says that for help given when none was given first, earth and heaven together are hardly repayment ('ஆற்றல் அரிது'). The giver's side and the receiver's side meet: the giver asks for nothing, and the receiver is told that nothing would be enough.

211 uses the rain cloud (மாரி) as the model of one who gives to the world and gets nothing back. 1010 uses it again: the short-lived want of the renowned rich is like the rain cloud running dry ('மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது'). The same figure covers both the giving and its interruption; Parimelazhagar on 1010 takes the simile to imply that such poverty passes quickly and the giving resumes.

211 says duty-giving seeks no return (கைம்மாறு). 221, opening the next chapter, defines giving as giving to those who have nothing, and says everything else has the nature of 'குறியெதிர்ப்பை', a measured loan to be returned. 221 turns 211's point into a test: a gift that looks to a return is not giving.

212 says all the wealth produced by exertion ('தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருள்') is for doing 'வேளாண்மை', benefaction. 613 says the proud distinction called benefaction ('வேளாண்மை என்னும் செருக்கு') rests in the quality called exertion ('தாளாண்மை'). The same two words are paired from opposite ends: in the Book of Virtue helping others is the purpose of earning, and in the Book of Wealth effort is the basis that makes helping possible.

212 ends 'வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு': earned wealth exists for the sake of benefaction. 81 ends on the same words: all of staying at home and keeping a household is for the sake of tending guests and doing them good. The household in 81 and wealth in 212 are given the same purpose in the same formula.

212 says wealth is for benefaction, with 'தக்கார்க்கு' read by Manakkudavar and Kalaignar as the worthy who receive it and by Parimelazhagar as the worthy who own it. 1006 describes the failure of this purpose: one who neither enjoys his great wealth nor gives anything to the worthy ('தக்கார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்') is an affliction (ஏதம்) to it. 1006 uses 'தக்கார்க்கு' plainly of recipients, which supports the Manakkudavar reading of 212.

213: neither in the world of the gods nor here ('புத்தேள் உலகத்தும் ஈண்டும்') is it easy to find another good like ஒப்புரவு. 363: there is no excellent wealth here like not wanting, and nothing there equals it either ('ஈண்டில்லை ஆண்டும் அஃதொப்பது இல்'). The same two-world formula crowns benevolence in the householder's section and desirelessness in the renouncer's; taken literally the two superlatives compete, and the pairing shows each section naming its own highest good.

213 ranks ஒப்புரவு above anything to be had in the gods' world or this one. 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world ('மேலுலகம் இல்லெனினும் ஈதலே நன்று'). Both detach the worth of helping others from heaven as a reward: in 213 heaven holds nothing better, and in 222 the good stands even without heaven.

214: only one who knows what is fitting (ஒத்தது) lives, and anyone else is placed among the dead ('செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்'). 1001: one who has piled up great wealth and does not use it is dead ('செத்தான்'), with nothing left for him to do. 1001 gives a concrete case of 214's verdict in the chapter on useless wealth: the hoarder is the man who does not know ஒப்புரவு.

214 defines who truly lives ('உயிர்வாழ்வான்') by knowing and doing what is fitting toward others. 240 defines it by reputation: those who live without blame are the ones who live, and those who live without renown do not ('வாழாதவர்'). Both redefine being alive by a social measure and count the rest as not living; the chapters on benevolence, giving and renown run in sequence.

Parimelazhagar reads 'ஒத்தது' in 214 as the way of the world (உலகநடை): one who knows and follows it lives. 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world ('உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்') lack understanding however much they have studied. On that reading both make accord with the world the test of a person, of being alive in 214 and of having understanding in 140; Manakkudavar instead takes ஒத்தது as ஒப்புரவு itself.

215: the wealth of the greatly wise man is like the village drinking tank filled with water ('ஊருணி நீர்நிறைந்தற்று'). 523: the life of one who does not mingle with his kin is like a tank filling with water without a bank ('குளவளாக் கோடின்றி நீர்நிறைந்தற்று'). The same phrase 'நீர்நிறைந்தற்று' is used both ways: a full tank that the village drinks from, and a full tank that holds nothing because the man is cut off from his people.

216: wealth that comes to a man of நயன் is like a fruit-bearing tree ripening inside the town ('பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்று'). 1008: the wealth of a man no one seeks out is like a poison tree ripening in the middle of the town ('நடுவூருள் நச்சுமரம் பழுத்தற்று'). The second is the first image reversed, a tree in the same place whose fruit no one can use; Manakkudavar reads 'நயனுடையான்' in 216 as one whom others desire, the exact opposite of 1008's 'நச்சப்படாதவன்'.

217 makes a tree the figure of a generous man's wealth: a tree that is medicine and does not fail ('மருந்தாகித் தப்பா மரம்'). 576 makes a tree the figure of people who have eyes but no kindly regard: they are like trees joined to the soil ('மண்ணோடு இயைந்த மரத்தனையர்'). The book uses the tree in two ways, for what gives to all who come to it and for what stands unmoved, so the image alone carries no fixed value.

218: even at a time without means ('இடனில் பருவத்தும்'), those who see what is due do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு. 955: even when what they have to give has shrunk ('வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும்'), an old family does not part from its character. The Book of Virtue credits this constancy to insight into duty ('கடனறி காட்சி'), and the Book of Wealth credits it to lineage ('பழங்குடி').

219: poverty, for a man of நயன், is being unable to do the things he is disposed to do ('செயும் நீர செய்யாது அமைகலா ஆறு'); Parimelazhagar adds that it is not the loss of his own enjoyments. 230: nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is not possible ('ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை'). 230 pushes 219's point further: for such a person the inability to give is worse than death.

219 redefines poverty for the benevolent man: it is not lacking goods but being unable to do good with them. 89 redefines it from the other side: poverty in the midst of having ('உடைமையுள் இன்மை') is the folly of not tending guests. In both verses poverty is measured by what one does for others and not by what one holds.

220: if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth getting even by selling oneself ('விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது உடைத்து'). 780: a death at which the eyes of one's lord fill with tears is worth getting even by begging ('இரந்துகோள் தக்கது உடைத்து'). The same closing formula takes something normally shunned, ruin or death, and declares it worth a degrading price, once for the benefactor and once for the soldier.

220 says ruin brought on by ஒப்புரவு is worth buying with oneself, and 218 says the dutiful do not slacken even without means. 480, in the chapter on knowing one's strength, warns that benevolence that does not weigh the limit of what one has ('உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புரவாண்மை') quickly ends one's wealth; Parimelazhagar comments that even ஒப்புரவு should not be overdone. They conflict if 220 is read as endorsing giving past one's means; on Manakkudavar's reading of 220, which treats the loss as a trade that pays later, the conflict is over whether that loss is a loss at all.

220 speaks of a man selling himself ('ஒருவன் விற்றுக்கோள்') as a price worth paying for the ruin that benevolence brings. 1080 says the base are fit for one thing: when something befalls them, to sell themselves quickly ('விற்றற்கு உரியர் விரைந்து'). Self-sale is honourable in the first as the cost of giving and contemptible in the second as an escape from one's own trouble.
